topics.title: Quadratic Trinomial Factorisation & Difference of Two Squares
topics.summary: Factorising ax² + bx + c by splitting the middle term, grouping in pairs, and a² - b² = (a - b)(a + b).
keyFormulas: ax² + bx + c: find p, q such that p+q = b and pq = ac
sourceNotes: Always check for a common factor across all terms before attempting quadratic trinomial or difference-of-squares factorisation.
For ax² + bx + c where a ≠ 1, find two integers whose product is a×c and whose sum is b, split bx into those two terms, and factorise by grouping.
When extracting a negative factor from the second pair in grouping, flip the sign inside the parentheses: -3x + 6 = -3(x - 2).
topics.workedExample: Factorise 2x² + 7x + 3: Product ac = 6, sum b = 7 -> numbers are 6 and 1. Rewrite as 2x² + 6x + x + 3 = 2x(x + 3) + 1(x + 3) = (2x + 1)(x + 3).
topics.commonMisconception: Sign distribution error when factoring out a negative common factor: writing 2x(x - 3) - 5(x + 3) instead of 2x(x - 3) - 5(x - 3).
learningObjectives: Factorising ax² + bx + c by splitting the middle term, grouping in pairs, and a² - b² = (a - b)(a + b).

topics.title: Simultaneous Linear Equations (Elimination & Substitution)
topics.summary: Solving systems of two linear equations algebraically and interpreting the intersection point graphically.
keyFormulas: Elimination: Match coefficients of x or y, then add/subtract
Substitution: Isolate one variable and substitute into the other equation
sourceNotes: In the elimination method, if the matching coefficients have opposite signs (+2y and -2y), ADD the equations; if they have the same sign (+2y and +2y), SUBTRACT one from the other.
Always verify your solution by substituting both (x, y) back into BOTH original equations.
topics.workedExample: Solve 2x + y = 11 and x - y = 1: Add the two equations to eliminate y -> 3x = 12 -> x = 4. Substitute x = 4 into 2(4) + y = 11 -> y = 3.
topics.commonMisconception: Adding equations when the variable to eliminate has identical signs instead of subtracting.
learningObjectives: Solving systems of two linear equations algebraically and interpreting the intersection point graphically.

topics.title: Fractional/Negative Indices & Standard Form (A × 10ⁿ)
topics.summary: Evaluating negative and fractional powers a^(-n) = 1/a^n, a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)^m, and scientific notation.
sourceNotes: A negative exponent indicates the reciprocal of the base raised to the positive exponent — it never makes the result negative.
In a^(m/n), the denominator n is the root and the numerator m is the power. Take the root first to keep numbers small!
topics.workedExample: Evaluate 27^(-2/3): Reciprocal gives 1 / 27^(2/3). Cube root of 27 is 3, then square it: 3² = 9. Result = 1/9.
topics.commonMisconception: Writing 27^(-2/3) as a negative number (-9) instead of the reciprocal 1/9.
learningObjectives: Evaluating negative and fractional powers a^(-n) = 1/a^n, a^(m/n) = (ⁿ√a)^m, and scientific notation.

topics.title: Kinematics: Velocity-Time Graphs, Acceleration & Free Fall
topics.summary: Displacement vs. distance, velocity vs. speed, gradient and area under v-t graphs, and g = 9.8 m/s².
sourceNotes: On a velocity-time (v-t) graph, the gradient (slope) equals acceleration, and the area enclosed under the graph equals total distance traveled.
Near Earth's surface in the absence of air resistance, all objects fall with constant acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m/s² (or 10 m/s²).
topics.workedExample: A car accelerates uniformly from 10 m/s to 26 m/s in 4 s. Acceleration a = (26 - 10)/4 = 4 m/s². Distance = ½(10 + 26) × 4 = 72 m.
topics.commonMisconception: Using d = v × t when velocity is changing instead of calculating the trapezium/triangle area under the v-t graph.
learningObjectives: Displacement vs. distance, velocity vs. speed, gradient and area under v-t graphs, and g = 9.8 m/s².

topics.title: Newton's Laws of Motion, Resultant Force & Moments
topics.summary: Balanced vs. unbalanced forces, F = ma, terminal velocity, and the principle of moments (τ = F × d).
keyFormulas: Moment of a Force: M = F × d_perp
sourceNotes: Newton's First Law: if resultant force is zero, a stationary object stays at rest AND a moving object continues at constant velocity in a straight line.
For rotational equilibrium, both the net force AND the net moment about any pivot must equal zero.
topics.workedExample: A 1,200 kg car experiences a forward engine thrust of 3,500 N and resistive drag of 1,100 N. F_net = 3,500 - 1,100 = 2,400 N. Acceleration a = 2,400 / 1,200 = 2.0 m/s².
topics.commonMisconception: Believing a constant forward resultant force is needed to maintain constant velocity (zero resultant force maintains constant velocity).
learningObjectives: Balanced vs. unbalanced forces, F = ma, terminal velocity, and the principle of moments (τ = F × d).

topics.title: Atomic Structure, Isotopes, Ionic & Covalent Bonding
topics.summary: Protons, neutrons, electrons, electronic configurations, dot-and-cross diagrams, and lattice structures.
sourceNotes: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons (atomic number) but different numbers of neutrons.
Ionic compounds (like NaCl, MgO) form giant ionic lattices with strong electrostatic attraction, giving them high melting points and electrical conductivity only when molten or aqueous.
topics.workedExample: Chlorine has two main isotopes: 75% Cl-35 and 25% Cl-37. Relative atomic mass Ar = (0.75 × 35) + (0.25 × 37) = 26.25 + 9.25 = 35.5.
topics.commonMisconception: Saying ionic compounds conduct electricity via free electrons when molten (they conduct via mobile ions, not free electrons!).
learningObjectives: Protons, neutrons, electrons, electronic configurations, dot-and-cross diagrams, and lattice structures.

topics.title: Enzymes (Lock-and-Key), Osmosis & Active Transport
topics.summary: Biological catalysts, denaturation by temperature/pH, water potential gradients, and active uptake.
keyFormulas: Osmosis: Net movement of H₂O from higher to lower water potential across a partially permeable membrane
sourceNotes: Enzymes are biological protein catalysts with a specific 3D active site complementary to their substrate (lock-and-key / induced fit).
Above optimum temperature, thermal agitation breaks intramolecular bonds, permanently denaturing the active site shape.
topics.workedExample: A potato cylinder placed in concentrated sucrose solution loses mass because water molecules move out of the cells by osmosis down the water potential gradient, causing plasmolysis.
topics.commonMisconception: Saying enzymes are 'killed' at high temperatures (enzymes are proteins, not living organisms — they are denatured).
learningObjectives: Biological catalysts, denaturation by temperature/pH, water potential gradients, and active uptake.

topics.title: Binary, Hexadecimal, ASCII & Logic Gates (AND, OR, NOT, XOR)
topics.summary: Binary conversion, two's complement, hexadecimal addressing, truth tables, and combined Boolean logic gate circuits.
learningObjectives: Convert positive and negative integers between denary, binary (8-bit two's complement) and hexadecimal
Construct and evaluate truth tables for complex logic circuits incorporating NOT, AND, OR, NAND, NOR, and XOR gates
keyFormulas: Hexadecimal Nibble: 4 binary bits = 1 hex digit (0-9, A-F where A=10, F=15)
Two's Complement: Invert all bits (0<->1) and add 1 to the least significant bit
XOR Gate: Output 1 when inputs are strictly different (A⊕B = A·B̄ + Ā·B)
sourceNotes: Hexadecimal is widely used in computer science because it is human-readable shorthand for long binary sequences (e.g., MAC addresses, HTML hex colors).
Two's complement ensures that addition and subtraction circuitry in the ALU use the identical hardware adder.
Truth tables list all 2ⁿ possible input combinations systematically in standard binary counting order (00, 01, 10, 11).
topics.workedExample: Convert -42 to 8-bit two's complement: +42 in binary = 00101010. One's complement (invert) = 11010101. Add 1 = 11010110.
topics.commonMisconception: Forgetting that the most significant bit (MSB) in signed two's complement represents negative place value (-128 in 8-bit).

topics.title: Quadratic Equations, Completing the Square & Quadratic Formula
topics.summary: Solving ax² + bx + c = 0 by factorisation, completing the square a(x + p)² + q, and the quadratic formula.
keyFormulas: Turning Point of a(x - h)² + k is (h, k)
sourceNotes: Always rearrange a quadratic equation into standard form ax² + bx + c = 0 before applying the zero-product property or quadratic formula.
The discriminant Δ = b² - 4ac determines root nature: Δ > 0 gives 2 distinct real roots; Δ = 0 gives 1 repeated real root; Δ < 0 gives no real roots.
topics.commonMisconception: Writing -b² instead of (-b)² when b is negative (e.g., evaluating (-5)² as -25 instead of +25 inside the square root).
learningObjectives: Solving ax² + bx + c = 0 by factorisation, completing the square a(x + p)² + q, and the quadratic formula.

topics.title: Trigonometry: SOH CAH TOA, Sine/Cosine Rules & Bearings
topics.summary: Right-triangle ratios, non-right triangles (Sine Rule, Cosine Rule, Area = ½ab sin C), and 3-figure bearings.
keyFormulas: Sine Rule: a/sin A = b/sin B
Cosine Rule: a² = b² + c² - 2bc cos A
sourceNotes: Use SOH CAH TOA only for right-angled triangles. For general triangles, use the Sine Rule when given a matching side-angle pair, and the Cosine Rule when given SAS or SSS.
Three-figure bearings are always measured clockwise from North (000° to 360°).
topics.workedExample: In triangle ABC, b = 8 cm, c = 10 cm, and included angle A = 60°. Area = ½ × 8 × 10 × sin(60°) = 40 × 0.866 = 34.6 cm².
topics.commonMisconception: Applying SOH CAH TOA to a non-right-angled triangle or forgetting leading zeros in bearings (writing 45° instead of 045°).
learningObjectives: Right-triangle ratios, non-right triangles (Sine Rule, Cosine Rule, Area = ½ab sin C), and 3-figure bearings.

topics.title: Circle Theorems, Vectors in 2D & Matrices
topics.summary: Angle at center vs. circumference, cyclic quadrilaterals, tangent-radius, position vectors, and 2×2 matrix inverse.
keyFormulas: Angle at Center = 2 × Angle at Circumference
Opposite angles in Cyclic Quad sum to 180°
sourceNotes: The angle subtended by an arc at the center of a circle is twice the angle subtended at any point on the remaining circumference.
A 2×2 matrix [a b; c d] has inverse (1/(ad - bc)) × [d -b; -c a], provided the determinant ad - bc ≠ 0.
topics.commonMisconception: Swapping the wrong diagonal elements or forgetting to negate b and c when finding a 2×2 matrix inverse.
learningObjectives: Angle at center vs. circumference, cyclic quadrilaterals, tangent-radius, position vectors, and 2×2 matrix inverse.

topics.title: Work, Energy, Power & Efficiency
topics.summary: Conservation of energy, kinetic energy KE = ½mv², gravitational potential energy ΔEp = mgh, and mechanical power.
keyFormulas: Power: P = W / t = ΔE / t
sourceNotes: Because KE is proportional to v², doubling an object's speed quadruples its kinetic energy (and quadruples braking distance for a constant braking force).
When a pendulum or roller coaster descends without friction, gravitational potential energy converts directly into kinetic energy: mgh = ½mv² -> v = √(2gh).
topics.workedExample: A 2 kg ball is dropped from a height of 5 m (g = 10 m/s²). Initial GPE = 2 × 10 × 5 = 100 J. Just before impact, KE = 100 J -> ½(2)v² = 100 -> v = 10 m/s.
topics.commonMisconception: Thinking doubling speed only doubles kinetic energy (it increases KE by a factor of 2² = 4).
learningObjectives: Conservation of energy, kinetic energy KE = ½mv², gravitational potential energy ΔEp = mgh, and mechanical power.

topics.title: DC Circuits, Ohm's Law, Electrical Power & Electromagnetism
topics.summary: Current I = Q/t, EMF/potential difference, V = IR, series vs. parallel resistors, and transformers.
keyFormulas: Power: P = V × I = I²R = V²/R
sourceNotes: In a series circuit, current I is the same everywhere and voltage divides across components; in a parallel circuit, voltage V is the same across branches and current splits.
Adding a resistor in parallel always REDUCES the total combined resistance because it opens an additional conducting path.
topics.workedExample: Two resistors of 6 Ω and 3 Ω are connected in parallel across a 12 V battery. 1/R_eq = 1/6 + 1/3 = 3/6 -> R_eq = 2 Ω. Total current I = 12 V / 2 Ω = 6 A.
topics.commonMisconception: Forgetting to take the reciprocal at the end when calculating parallel resistance (leaving R_eq as 3/6 = 0.5 Ω instead of 6/3 = 2 Ω).
learningObjectives: Current I = Q/t, EMF/potential difference, V = IR, series vs. parallel resistors, and transformers.

topics.title: The Mole Concept, Stoichiometry & Electrolysis
topics.summary: Avogadro's constant, molar mass, molar gas volume (24 dm³ at r.t.p.), limiting reactants, and redox at electrodes.
keyFormulas: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain
sourceNotes: At room temperature and pressure (r.t.p.), 1 mole of any ideal gas occupies 24 dm³ (24,000 cm³).
In electrolysis, cations (positive ions) migrate to the negative cathode where they are reduced; anions migrate to the positive anode where they are oxidized.
topics.workedExample: Calculate the volume of H₂ gas at r.t.p. produced when 2.4 g of Magnesium (Ar = 24) reacts with excess HCl (Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl₂ + H₂): Moles Mg = 2.4/24 = 0.1 mol. Mole ratio 1:1 -> 0.1 mol H₂ × 24 dm³/mol = 2.4 dm³.
topics.commonMisconception: Forgetting to convert cm³ to dm³ (dividing by 1,000) before using n = C × V in titration problems.
learningObjectives: Avogadro's constant, molar mass, molar gas volume (24 dm³ at r.t.p.), limiting reactants, and redox at electrodes.

topics.title: Von Neumann Architecture, Searching/Sorting & SQL Databases
topics.summary: Fetch-Decode-Execute cycle, registers (PC, MAR, MDR, CIR, ACC), Linear/Binary search, Bubble sort, and SQL SELECT.
keyFormulas: FDE Cycle: PC -> MAR -> Memory -> MDR -> CIR -> Control Unit -> ACC
SQL: SELECT fields FROM table WHERE condition ORDER BY field
sourceNotes: In the Fetch-Decode-Execute cycle, the Program Counter (PC) holds the address of the next instruction, copies it to MAR, fetches the instruction into MDR and CIR, and increments PC.
Binary search divides the search space in half each step (O(log n)), but requires the array to be sorted first.
topics.workedExample: To retrieve names of students in Grade 10 scoring above 85 sorted highest first: SELECT StudentName, Score FROM Students WHERE Grade = 10 AND Score > 85 ORDER BY Score DESC;
topics.commonMisconception: Applying binary search to an unsorted array without sorting it first.
learningObjectives: Fetch-Decode-Execute cycle, registers (PC, MAR, MDR, CIR, ACC), Linear/Binary search, Bubble sort, and SQL SELECT.

topics.title: Monohybrid Inheritance, DNA Structure & Ecosystem Energy Flow
topics.summary: Punnett squares, codominance, sex-linked inheritance, DNA double helix base pairing (A-T, G-C), and trophic energy pyramids.
learningObjectives: Predict the phenotypic and genotypic ratios of monohybrid crosses using genetic diagrams and Punnett squares
Explain energy losses between trophic levels and construct pyramids of biomass and energy
keyFormulas: Trophic Efficiency: Only ~10% of energy transfers to the next trophic level (90% lost as heat, respiration, unconsumed matter)
DNA Base Pairing Rule: Adenine (A) = Thymine (T), Guanine (G) ≡ Cytosine (C)
Heterozygous Cross: Tt × Tt -> 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt (3:1 dominant to recessive phenotype ratio)
sourceNotes: Phenotype is the physical expression of a trait; genotype is the genetic makeup of alleles.
Energy flow in ecosystems is unidirectional and non-cyclic, unlike nutrient cycles (carbon, nitrogen) which are continuously recycled.
A test cross involves breeding an organism of dominant phenotype with a homozygous recessive individual to determine its genotype.
topics.workedExample: Cross two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt × Tt). Gametes: T, t. Punnett Square results: TT (tall), Tt (tall), Tt (tall), tt (short). Phenotypic ratio: 3 tall : 1 short.
topics.commonMisconception: Assuming that dominant alleles are always more common or 'stronger' in an ecosystem than recessive alleles.
